note: Every claim this archive has published and then had to take back, with what was said, what is true, and how the mistake was made. It is kept because an archive that only shows its successes is not telling you how reliable it is. Corrections are made **in the place where the mistake was made**, not quietly on a back page — this list is the index to them.
lead: Twenty things this archive got wrong.

rows.what: I corrected a note that was right
rows.said: That the working notes' line — *«**55 suppressed charts** to review by hand»* — was stale and wrong, and that the true figure was **763 of 1,056 dossiers with no pedigree chart**: *«wrong by a factor of fourteen, in the direction that makes the job look nearly done»*.
rows.true:
**The note was right and I was measuring something else.** A dossier has three possible states, not two:

**238** have a chart drawn. **55** have candidate households that the **date gate rejected every one of** — a chart *suppressed*, which is exactly what the note said and exactly the pile that needs reviewing by hand. **763** have **no household link at all**, so there is nothing to suppress and nothing to draw.

55 is the review queue. 763 is not a backlog; it is the shape of the evidence.
rows.how:
`v.get("ptree")` was read as «has a chart». It is not: the builder returns a `ptree` object carrying **`none: True`** when it found candidates and the gate threw them all out. Conflating «suppressed» with «absent» turned a precise note into a false alarm — and the alarm was published in a commit that was itself about numbers going stale.

The audit now prints all three states separately. **Being loudly right about an error is not the same as being right**, and the check I built to stop numbers rotting produced a rotten number on its first day.

rows.what: Twenty-four households with the parents the wrong way round
rows.said: Twenty-four of this archive's 112 households named a **De Franceschi woman as the father** and **her husband as the mother**. *«father: Michiela De Franceschi · mother: Domenico Giachin»*. Forty people's roster entries said things like *«**Domenico Giachin** — named as **mother** on 2 baptisms»*.
rows.true: Every one is inverted. The women are the mothers; the men are the fathers. **All 24 are De Franceschi daughters married out** — which is why the error clusters exactly where it does.
rows.how:
The households built from the FamilySearch index take the two parent names the index returns and assign them **by position**, not by sex. Where the De Franceschi parent was listed first — which is what happens when the *mother* is the one carrying this archive's surname — the pair went in backwards.

**So the bug bit precisely the people this archive is worst at tracking.** The whole Vodnjan argument is that «the surname keeps its sons and loses its daughters»; twenty-four married-out daughters were in the data and the data had them down as men.

Found while testing something else entirely — chasing whether one **Michiela De Franceschi fu Giuseppe** was a daughter of the Giuseppe this archive already documents. The check that found it is now in `scripts/audit.py` and runs on every publish: **a female given name in the father field**. It would have caught this the day it was introduced.

rows.what: Counted four candidates and could name three
rows.said: That **four** look-alike candidates had been examined at full magnification and given up on this film — *«q.m Francesco»*, *«di Francesco»*, *«da Francesche»*, «and one more».
rows.true: There are **three**. *«Nicolò Sussani q.m Francesco»* and *«Antonia Palin di Francesco»* on image 560, and *«Bonetta da Francesche»* at page 164, entry 21. There is no fourth.
rows.how:
A running tally kept in the head rather than in the file. The sentence was written, the fourth could not be named, and it went out anyway with «and one more» standing in for evidence.

Small, and caught within the minute — but it is the same shape as the mistake that put **1,952** on this site: **a number written before it was counted**. The count of things given up is exactly as much a claim as the count of things found, and this archive's whole argument is that it keeps both.

rows.what: Full-text result counts that were a year, not a count
rows.said: That FamilySearch's full-text search returned **1,952 results for *Gologorica*, 1,719 for *Gračišće* and 1,885 for *Defranceschi*** — and, noting how implausibly alike those three numbers were, that they «**have not been tested**» and should not be trusted.
rows.true:
Every one of the three is wrong, and the real figures are not close.

**Gologorica returns 19.** *Gračišće* three pages. *Crikvenica* fifteen. *Ližnjan* **two**. **Defranceschi returns about 9,900** — **five times** what was published, not a fifth of it. And **Vodnjan returns nothing at all**: the Croatian name post-dates every record in the corpus, which uses **Dignano** — about 12,200 of those, most of them the *other* Dignano, in Friuli.
rows.how:
The number was scraped with a loose pattern — `([0-9,]+)\s*Results` — off a page whose visible text ends *«… Border Crossing Records 1924-**1952**\nResults per page:»*. **It matched a year out of a collection title.** «1,952 results» was a border-crossing collection's end date standing next to the words «Results per page».

What makes this worse than a scraping bug: **the page said the numbers looked wrong and published them anyway.** Three unrelated searches returning numbers of the same size was called «the shape of a number that counts something other than what you think» — and then the one check that would have settled it, *look at how many results are actually on the page*, was not run. It takes one request.

**Flagging a doubt is not the same as resolving it.** A figure you have publicly called untrustworthy should not be in the sentence at all.

The finding underneath is unharmed and is better than it looked: **19 hits for Gologorica is a set small enough to read end to end**, which is exactly what makes the village sweep worth doing.

rows.what: A correction that never reached the data file
rows.said: The families page described the southern-Istrian family as «**Southern Istria — Pula, Fažana, Ližnjan**», resting on the name being «**in the Pula registers from 1667**».
rows.true: Those entries are from the **Svetvinčenat** register, DGS 005497884, and the parish carries the surname from **1657**. Pula holds ten register entries of the name, only three accepted, and four of them are spelt **Bellulovich Francessich** — a different surname.
rows.how: The correction itself was made days ago and published **on the lines chart**. It never reached `families.json`, which went on asserting the original claim in its own title. **This is the second time in this archive that a published correction has failed to reach the data behind it** — the first cost forty-four people their parish. Found by auditing the chart's place labels against every place string in the register, the roster and the households, which is a check that should run on a schedule and does not.

rows.what: Numbers I gave David before checking them
rows.said: That **Pula** had «about fifty records» and that **Krk, Kastav and Oprtalj** were towns missing from the lines chart.
rows.true: Pula has **ten** in the register. The fifty came from adding register, roster and households together and folding «Pola» into «Pula» — three different kinds of row counted as one kind. And Krk, Kastav and Oprtalj are **not gaps at all**: the surnames there are **Franceschini** and **Francetich**, different stocks of a different name.
rows.how: Caught before publishing, by recounting per source and printing the **spelling column** beside each place. The lesson is the one this archive keeps meeting from a new direction: **a place count means nothing until you have looked at what surname is actually standing in it.**

rows.what: A filter of mine deleted a paragraph of hers
rows.said: Nothing — that is the problem. The account of **Paputchka's death**, some five hundred words, **silently vanished from the transcription**.
rows.true: The scanner destroyed its opening sentence, returning *«WS CAPES FUG PS PEPE AU SII Pony FRU. OI WC PI PO UT UU TET»* where she had written *«We experienced "true" love with our Siberian Husky Paputchka»*. A rule I wrote to strip scanner noise matched that line — and because prose is stored **one line per paragraph**, deleting the line deleted **the entire paragraph**.
rows.how:
Restored word for word from the original, supplied by David, and **marked on the page** as restored so no reader has to wonder which text they are looking at.

The lesson is specific and unpleasant: **a cleanup rule that operates on a whole paragraph can destroy a whole paragraph.** Noise-stripping must be scoped to the noise — a few tokens — and never to the container it sits in. It was also **found by the reader, not by me**: nothing in the build warned that five hundred words had gone, because nothing was counting.

**A reconciliation was then run over the whole page** — every substantial line of the raw scan tested against the published text — and it found **four more losses of the same kind**: the closing paragraph of the husky piece, which had been left beginning mid-sentence at *«anger and rage»*; a sentence from *A Suicide Avenged*; a line of dialogue from it; and part of the godparents letter. All four are restored and marked. **One passage is unrecoverable** — three lines describing a person, from the 2004 course — and stands on the page as a stated gap rather than a silent one.

rows.what: A living man named in an allegation
rows.said: Her own introduction to the first poem was published word for word, and it **named the man she was then married to** in a sentence describing *«a long standing affair, committing adultery for years»*.
rows.true: **That should never have gone up.** It is an allegation of adultery against a **named living person**, published by this archive. That the words are hers and that she published them herself does not transfer the risk or the discretion — the archive chose to reproduce them.
rows.how:
The name is removed; the sentence now reads *«my marriage was over»*. It is **the single alteration to her text anywhere on that page**, and the page says so.

The failure was not ignorance of the rule. **The same rule had been applied an hour earlier**, and correctly, to a different document — a statement of allegations that was excluded entirely for naming living people. Then a transcription was published verbatim without running the same test over it. **A rule applied once is not a rule; it has to be run against every page that goes out.**

rows.what: «Corsica — not ours»
rows.said: The lines page filed Corsica under «**not ours**».
rows.true: **Nobody had checked.** Not one search had ever been run in a French archive for this surname, in any commune. «Not ours» was a **guess wearing the clothes of a finding** — the same error as a false join, made in the opposite direction.
rows.how: Replaced with a stated position and its reasoning on a page of its own: a **parallel, not a branch**, expected to be unrelated and **not yet tested**. **Dismissing a line without looking is exactly as unevidenced as claiming one.**

rows.what: «Nine parishes» on the Archive page
rows.said: «**1,151 registers catalogued across nine parishes**» — the count of books was computed from the data, the count of parishes was typed by hand.
rows.true: There are **fourteen**: Barban, Cerovlje, Gologorica, Gračišće, Ližnjan, Motovun, Pazin, Pićan, Poreč, Svetvinčenat, Umag, Vižinada, Vodnjan and Čepić.
rows.how: Now computed from the same data as the number beside it. **Any figure a page states should be derived, not typed** — a hand-typed number is right on the day it is written and wrong from then on.

rows.what: What the Archive's 1,151 actually counts
rows.said: Nothing false — but the page led with **1,151** and let a reader assume it was a measure of the project's reach. Set beside a sister site's **10,536 records naming 4,779 people**, it invited exactly the wrong comparison.
rows.true: **1,151 counts books, not people.** It is the Pazin inventory of parish registers that exist. This archive has opened a book in **7 of the 14 parishes**, and most of the **997 digitised** volumes have never been looked at. The comparable people-counts are **1,136** on Everyone and **1,508** on The Register.
rows.how: The page now says so in its own words, and says why the sister project's number is larger: it **read a town's death registers act by act** rather than searching an index for one surname. **1,151 is not an achievement. It is the size of the job.**

rows.what: Piero della Francesca in the family tree
rows.said: Nothing on this site — the claim is in **the family's own MyHeritage tree**, which places the painter **Piero della Francesca (1415–1492)** of Sansepolcro in this family, with his father Benedetto and mother Romana di Perino.
rows.true: Piero's father genuinely was a **de' Franceschi** of Sansepolcro, so the surname is real. **The connection to the Carnian and Istrian family is not.** Nothing documents it, and nothing here claims it.
rows.how: Recorded rather than deleted, because the tree is a source this archive reads and it is better to name a doubtful join than to leave it unmentioned. All three are marked so on their own pages. **This is the third famous namesake the project has had to refuse** — after the Venetian printer and the Venetian painter — and the pattern is always the same: a well-known man of the name, and no join but the name.

rows.what: Hedviga Blažević has two birthdays
rows.said: Two pages give her birth as **8 March 1926**. A third page quotes the certified extract of the Senj birth register, attached to her son's 1951 entry, which gives **3 August 1926**.
rows.true: **Both have stood on this site at once and nobody noticed.** Written as numbers they are **8/3/1926** and **3/8/1926** — a day and a month exchanged, almost certainly where a European date met an English-speaking translator. This archive does not know which is right.
rows.how: **Neither has been quietly deleted.** Both now stand, marked as in conflict, and the Senj birth register for 1926 is an errand. The lesson is one this project keeps relearning: **a date that appears twice in an archive should be diffed, not trusted twice.**

rows.what: Anton Rudolf, dead in 1943 and certified in 1950
rows.said: Anton Rudolf Defranceski, born 20 January 1890 at Klenovica house 22, **died in 1943** — recorded here «per the family». The same page also has him **on the Pfullingen list of foreigners in 1947** and **certified by that town's mayor in 1950**.
rows.true: **Those cannot both be about the same living man.** Either the 1943 death is wrong — and it was only ever family testimony, never a register — or the Pfullingen documents are about a different Anton. The archive printed both and did not notice.
rows.how: Surfaced only because the family's oral history of **1948** made the widow's situation matter. Written up on Nineteen forty-eight, and the Crikvenica death register for 1943 is now an errand. **Lore is worth collecting partly because it makes you re-read your own pages.**

rows.what: What the first 403 actually was
rows.said: That FamilySearch's tile server had **blocked** the death-register reading, recorded as `blocked` in the Search Register and written up on Method as a second instance of *when the service says stop, stop*.
rows.true:
**The tile path was wrong.** Tiles live at `…/image.xml`'s sibling `image_files/{level}/{col}_{row}.jpg`, and the reader was asking for `…/{level}/{col}_{row}.jpg` — no `image_files`. Today that same wrong path returns a plain **404**; yesterday the security service answered the unknown path with a **403**. So the reading was stopped by **my own broken URL**, dressed up as somebody else's refusal.

A real block did come later, after several hundred tile requests, on `image.xml` itself — and *that* one is recorded honestly.
rows.how: **Check that the request is well-formed before concluding you have been refused.** A 403 on a path that does not exist is not a verdict on your conduct. The cheap test — does the *correct* URL work? — costs one request and was not run.

rows.what: The FamilySearch paging cap
rows.said: A method note stated the persona endpoint caps out at about **1,100 records**.
rows.true: The real ceiling is about **1,800**. The 1,100 figure came from a run that stopped early and was never retested; the full harvest of 10 September reached 1,800 distinct records before the endpoint began serving page one again.
rows.how: Retested deliberately, at offsets 1,800, 2,600 and 3,600, before publishing a number that the whole of The Register now rests on.

rows.what: Living people
rows.said: The footer of every page read **«Living people are excluded from this build.»**
rows.true: At David's instruction the policy changed: living people the archive knows of are now named, **by name only** — no date of birth, no address, no place of residence, no photograph.
rows.how: The footer was corrected the same day the policy changed, rather than left contradicting the pages above it.

rows.what: A face on the direct line
rows.said: A hand-tinted portrait of a bearded man in a bow tie, published as **Josip Defranceschi, born at Gračišće 22 March 1863** — David's great-grandfather, and the only likeness the direct line had.
rows.true: It is from the **Imotski** branch, and the sitter is a Josip of that family. **No likeness of the Crikvenica Josip is known to this archive.** The companion portrait published as his wife Ana is withdrawn too, because its only identification was that it matched the man beside it.
rows.how: Two branches' photographs sit in one family collection. A card carried the name, this line has a man of that name, and this archive matched the face to the name without asking which Josip — while checking every register plate on the same page against Pazin and Ledenice. **The portrait was never checked against anything.** Identified by David, who holds the originals. The retired 2018 GEDCOM spliced Imotski onto this line as well: the same seam has caught this archive twice.

rows.what: Seventy-eight records moved to the wrong parish
rows.said: That the seventy-eight Vodnjan records were **really Vižinada's**, because resolving them to film 005497893 and asking the catalogue who made that film returned «Rimokatolička crkva. Župa Vižinada».
rows.true: **A reel can carry more than one parish.** That one holds Vižinada's deaths 1754–1831 *and* **Vodnjan's baptisms 1815–1866** (koha:963267). The records are Vodnjan's.
rows.how: The catalogue answers a film-number query with the **first creator on the reel**. The method was sound and the question put to it was wrong. It stood on the site for about an hour, published within twenty minutes of being reached and **without a single image being opened**. What made it look right: the one death on that reel really is Vižinada's — it is in the *Liber Defunctorum of Castellier*, Kaštelir.

rows.what: Forty-four people filed under the wrong town
rows.said: Eight reconstructed Vodnjan households and their children carried **Vižinada** as their parish in the roster, and the households themselves had no place at all.
rows.true: They are Vodnjan. Eight households placed, **forty-four rows moved**, and Vodnjan moved out of *unplaced* into Southern Istria.
rows.how: The correction above was published on the narrative page and **never reached the data**. David asked why the headcount had not moved all day; it had not, because the roster was three commits behind the research and still carried the error the essay had already retracted. Fixed, and the rebuild order is now written into the queue notes.

rows.what: A surname misread
rows.said: «**Alvise Bortolan** q.m Saba», husband of Lucia De Franceschi, in two published entries.
rows.true: «**Alvise Birattan** q.m Saba». The 1825 entry writes it legibly, and the two earlier ones say the same thing once you go back and look.
rows.how: A hard hand read twice from the same wrong first guess. *Bortolan* was this archive's word, not the register's.

rows.what: A marriage dated forty years early
rows.said: Carlo De Franceschi × Maria Michelcich, **1812**.
rows.true: **1 March 1852**, Rovinj, entry 31. The bride was twenty-six, so she cannot have married in 1812.
rows.how: Carried straight from an index whose year field appears to hold the groom's, not the marriage's. It survived because nobody had opened the image — the same failure as the portrait, in a different medium.

rows.what: A broken site pushed live
rows.said: Nothing — the page simply was not there for about six minutes.
rows.true: The build had failed and the commit went out anyway.
rows.how: `npm run build | tail -2` hides the build's exit code behind the pipe's. **This was the second time.** There is now `scripts/publish.sh`, which builds without a pipe, checks that every source page produced an output file, and refuses to commit or push if either fails.

rows.what: An opening said to hold nothing
rows.said: That opening 578 of the Svetvinčenat baptisms holds **no De Franceschi**.
rows.true: It does. The entry was found by resolving the index arks to their images rather than trusting the search result.
rows.how: An absence in an index was read as an absence in the register. The correction was published **underneath the original claim**, which is where it belongs.

rows.what: Two children who are one child
rows.said: Two boys named Piero, baptised nine days apart, counted as two people.
rows.true: One child, entered twice by the priest. The **godparent pair is identical** — Martino Salambat and Andriana Quelis — which is proof, not coincidence.
rows.how: Found by reading the openings rather than the index. The roster had already deduplicated by name and year, so the published count was right for the wrong reason; that too was stated.

rows.what: A petition attributed to the wrong person
rows.said: That the 1942 naturalisation petition filed as «Bruno de Franceschi Or Seedorf» was **Bruno's**.
rows.true: It is **Gerda's** — her declaration, carrying his name in the index because of the marriage.
rows.how: An index heading read as a subject.

rows.what: A column said to be unalignable
rows.said: That the «going to join» entries could not be aligned to the passengers.
rows.true: They align perfectly. **The image holds two ledger pages**, and those particular entries belong to the **Di Bruzzi** family, not to ours.
rows.how: A page boundary mistaken for a data problem.

rows.what: A line described as an open question
rows.said: Vodnjan: «twelve families in 1945 … accounted for by no existing line … the newest open question».
rows.true: **Five documented generations**, two separate lines, and four women of the name married out before the books open.
rows.how: Not wrong when written — overtaken, and left standing for hours after the evidence had changed. The lesson is the same as the roster's: a finding is not published until the data files carry it too.

rows.what: A pedigree spliced at the wrong join
rows.said: The **Imotski** family joined to David's own line, in the 2018 GEDCOM this archive inherited.
rows.true: They are separate. The GEDCOM is retired — 8,286 people against the live tree's 15,643, and David's own verdict: «really old and really wrong».
rows.how: An old export was trusted as a source. It is now used for nothing. Note how often Imotski turns up in this list.

rows.what: A register's own error, kept as it stands
rows.said: «Il Signor Carlo De Franceschi … celibe, **d'anni 40**», 1 March 1852.
rows.true: He was **forty-two**, born 16 October 1809.
rows.how: Not this archive's mistake but the register's, and it is transcribed as written rather than silently improved. Ages in these books are what somebody said in the room — and in this room the man being asked was too ill to stand up.

rows.what: Names that are not this name
rows.said: Nothing — these were caught before publication and are recorded so they are not found again.
rows.true: **Franceschich** of Buzet is a Slavic patronymic, not Franceschi. **Francin** is its own Vodnjan family — although Pietro De Franceschi's first wife was a Francin, so in that parish the two are a household deep in each other. **Pietro Francin q.m Dom.co de Rondel** is not a De Franceschi.
rows.how: Read by eye rather than matched by string. This is the whole argument for reading a register instead of querying one.

rows.what: Bold words breaking onto their own line
rows.said: Nothing wrong in the words — but wherever a paragraph of running prose contained a **bold phrase**, the phrase was thrown onto a line of its own, so the sentence read as three broken fragments.
rows.true: A styling fault, live across the site for an unknown period and on eleven pages that pass marked-up text into a paragraph.
rows.how: `.prose` was declared `display:flex; flex-direction:column`, which turns every inline child — including a `<strong>` — into its own flex item. It is now spacing applied between block children only. Found by looking at a new page rather than by any test. Two stylesheets exist in this repo and only one is loaded; the first fix went into the wrong one.

rows.what: Counting records by place, with a parameter that does not count
rows.said: Per-place record counts for this surname across sixty Istrian and Kvarner towns, and a research queue carrying «Vižinada — 53 records, unread», «Draguč — 25», «Dubrovnik — 38».
rows.true: **The place parameter on this search endpoint does not filter.** Ten values were tested, including «Zzzznowhere» and «Atlantis», and every one returned the same total: **3,652**. Vižinada and Draguč return identical result sets. Dubrovnik returns the unfiltered list. The queued «Vižinada 53» records are on the **Vodnjan** film and have already been read.
rows.how: The parameter is a relevance boost dressed as a filter — no error, no warning, just the whole set back in a different order. The sweep survives because its method independently checked each record's own place text before counting it; the **queue did not**, and carried three phantom tasks for days. The reliable route is to resolve records to their film and read the catalogue's item list — remembering that a film can carry more than one parish.

rows.what: «Never once as the officiant»
rows.said: That Don Stefano De Franceschi appears in the Vodnjan marriage register **nineteen times as a witness and never once as the officiant** — a point this archive made repeatedly, because it fixed his standing under the parroco Giovanni Tromba.
rows.true: On **26 January 1833** he married a couple himself: «**D.n Stefano De Franceschi, De Parochi lic., li congiunse e benedisse nella Chiesa Parrocchiale**».
rows.how: True of every entry from 1819 to the end of 1832, and stated as though it were true of the whole book — while sixty openings of that book were still unread. **A claim about a register nobody has finished reading is a claim about the part you have read.** What survives is the better point: he acts «De Parochi lic.», by the parish priest's licence, exactly as at the baptism of 1816. Seventeen years apart, the same three words.

rows.what: Reading a formula as a personal arrangement
rows.said: That «**De Parochi lic.**» — by the parish priest's licence — was the particular standing Don Stefano De Franceschi held at Vodnjan, and that the register used «the same three words about him» seventeen years apart, at a baptism in 1816 and at an altar in 1833.
rows.true: It is the register's **standard formula for any priest deputising for the parroco**. The very next entry, 13 February 1833, uses it of **Don Pietro Bradamante**.
rows.how: Published the day before, on a run of entries that happened to feature one man. Two consecutive days of the same book undid it. The underlying fact is unchanged — Don Stefano was never the parson of Vodnjan — but the phrase was doing work it does not do.

rows.what: Publishing this archive's own method back to it as a discovery
rows.said: That forty-five per cent of the indexed records carry no town, that the film number in each record is the way to a parish, and — presented as the day's lesson — that a reel can carry more than one parish, so the film is «a fast first pass and not an answer».
rows.true:
**All three were already on this site.** The parish-map section of the same page says the index «usually gives no parish… every persona carries the ark of the image it was read from, the service turns that ark into a DGS film number, and the catalogue names the film's parish». And the correction entry above it, from 9 September, already ends: «The reliable route is to resolve records to their film and read the catalogue's item list — *remembering that a film can carry more than one parish*.»

The 45% is a measurement of something this archive had already stated qualitatively. It was written up as though nobody here had noticed.
rows.how:
By not reading the page being added to. Four sections were appended to /istria-sweep/ in one afternoon without the existing parish-map section being read first — the same page, eighty lines further down.

**What is actually new, and it is narrower:** `q.fatherSurname` and `q.motherSurname` are honoured when either is the sole name term, which the reference note said was impossible and which took the pool from 954 records to 1,619; and resolving a record through its **image ark to the book waypoint** is finer than film-to-catalogue — it settles a two-parish reel *automatically* instead of requiring somebody to remember to check. The measurement that 110 of 112 records on film 005497893 are the second parish's is new. The idea is not.

rows.what: «The earliest the surname is indexed anywhere in Istria: Labin, 1615»
rows.said: That an **Aloÿsius Defranceschi** appears at Albona in **1615** — «sixty-four years before the Mione headmen's list, and eighty-five before the date Carlo gives for his family's arrival». Carried as one of three key findings of the September sweep, pinned on the atlas, and used as the outer bound of the family's presence in Istria.
rows.true:
**Three later measurements cannot find it.** The **rebuilt sweep** on the same page — written precisely because the first method matched a truncated field and stopped early — gives Labin **1789–1892**. The **by-image test** of 13 September gives **1826–1866**, and six of Labin's fourteen indexed hits are *Franceschich*, *Francescich*, *Francocich*, which are not this family. And this archive's own **register**, 1,508 rows each carrying the id the service returned for it, **holds no 1615 Labin row**; its only 1615 row is an *Andriana Franchini*.

So the 1615 exists in one place only: the table built by the method this page has already declared broken. **And the source of the number has since been found.** The only *Aloÿsius Defranceschi* in any harvest on disk is born **1790**, son of *Mathæus Defranceschi and Osvalda Labinaz or Dominj* — a **Vižinada** household. The *Gasparo De Franceschi* named beside him is in none of the data. And Labin's filmed volume list contains a book called «**Deaths (Umrli) 1615, 1585-1649**».

So the entry was a man from the wrong parish dated two centuries early, a man who does not exist, and **a date taken from a shelf-list instead of a record**. It is withdrawn, not merely disputed.

**What stands instead: Rovinj 1619, then Svetvinčenat 1628.** Both are in the register, both have an image behind them, and the second was read off the page the same morning.
rows.how:
By checking a load-bearing number against the archive's own data instead of against the page that first published it. The check cost one grep. It was prompted by writing a new place page for Labin and finding nothing in the register to put on it.

**Withdrawn the same day** after searching every harvest file for the name rather than only the published tables. That search cost one grep too, and should have been the first thing done rather than the second.

rows.what: Ten women shown as born in the year their own children were being baptised
rows.said: A birth year for each of ten married-in women — «b. 1822» for Lucia Bonassin, «b. 1816» for Maria Malusá, «b. 1841» for Maria Dorliguzzo, and seven more.
rows.true:
**None of those is a birth year.** Each woman is the *mother* of a household whose first child is baptised in that very year, or in one of the years she was already bearing children. Lucia Bonassin «b. 1822» is the mother in «Gio Maria De Franceschi × Lucia Bonassin, **1822**–1831». Maria Malusá «b. 1816» is the mother in «Pietro De Franceschi × Maria Malusá, **1816**–1824». Anna Defranceschi (Voran) «b. 1865» is the mother in a household running **1857–1865**.

The year is the first time she appears in the record — the baptism of her eldest known child. It was carried into the roster as a birth. **Nobody is born in the year their own child is born.**

All ten now show the year as a first appearance, with the birth recorded as unknown.
rows.how:
Found by asking why the pedigree gate was suppressing fifty-five charts. The gate was doing its job: it refuses a parent who would be under twelve at the first birth, and these women were failing that test **because their data said they were nought.** The charts were the symptom; the birth years were the fault.

**And one rule was tried and withdrawn inside the same hour.** Generalising it — *any* person whose recorded birth is less than twelve years before a household they parent — «corrected» **113 rows**, including an Antonio Defranceschi born 1897 attached to an 1825 household and a Josip Defranceski born 1947 attached to one from 1890. Those are not bad birth years; they are **name collisions**, which this archive proved the same morning when «Maria Defranceschi» turned out to be thirteen women in thirteen parishes. The rule assumed the match was right and the year wrong; in 103 of 113 cases it was the other way round. Reverted, and narrowed to the one case where the name form itself identifies a wife — «Maiden (Married)» — which no father and son can share.

rows.what: «Gio Batta De Franceschi and Zanetta Gravisi, parents of the groom»
rows.said: That the Šterna household ran **Gio Batta De Franceschi × Zanetta Gravisi**, and that their son Bortolo's marriage stood behind two entries in the book of 1723–1820. Published on the morning of 13 September, on the strength of the index's four names.
rows.true:
**Zanetta Gravisi is Bortolo's wife, not his mother.** The index lists groom, groom's father, bride and bride's father; this archive read four names as two couples.

The page reads: «Bortolo figlio del q. Gio: Batta de Franceschi **dalla Cargna**… ha contratto legitimo Matrimonio coll'Ill.ma Sig.a **Zanetta Gravisi** figlia dell'Ill.mo Sig.r **Marchese Nazario** della Villa di Cepich di questa Pieve», 12 November 1777.

And there was never a second marriage. The other «record» is a modern **archivist's pencil finding-aid slip** filmed with the book, which the index counted as a separate entry — and which independently confirms every word of the reading.
rows.how:
By opening the two images instead of reasoning about the index rows, which is what the same page had already said was the only reliable move. The correction was published the same day as the claim.

It is also the most valuable correction this archive has made, because going to the page produced the sentence the whole project has been missing: **an Istrian De Franceschi whose origin is written down**.

rows.what: Ten more birth years that are first-appearance dates
rows.said: Birth years for ten people who are parents in a Vodnjan household — «b. 1817» and «b. 1819» for a Pietro De Franceschi whose household runs 1816–1824, «b. 1822» and «b. 1830» for a Domenica whose household runs 1817–1832, and so on.
rows.true: Each year falls **inside the span during which that household was baptising children**, and each person is a parent in it. They are first-appearance dates. Twenty such years have now been corrected across the site.
rows.how:
The earlier pass used only the name form «Maiden (Married)», which is safe but narrow. This one adds two tests that let the rule reach further without repeating the morning's mistake of blanking 113 good years:

**The places must agree.** A row at Draguč matched to a household at Rijeka is a name collision, not a bad year — 59 of 121 candidates failed this and were left alone.

**The year must fall inside the childbearing span.** Place agreement is not enough on its own, because Vodnjan recycles the same six Christian names across generations: a *Pietro De Franceschi b. 1858* sits at the same place as a Pietro whose household ran 1816–1824, and he is a grandson, not a bad date. **Eighteen were skipped on this test**, all but three of them at Vodnjan.

Ten survived both. The rule is now narrow enough to state: a person who is a parent in a household, at the same place, whose recorded birth falls within the years that household was bearing children, has a first appearance recorded as a birth.
